body: I noticed a few PRs related to focus by @Rindbee so perhaps they know precisely what's going on here?
May be related to #103898 but seemed distinct enough for me to make two issue reports.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/56836f2f-1c9e-4b3e-bc07-1410e4fdca7f)

Because the one on the right has a closer point, it does not enter the second step: the direction correction stage. Similar to moving the focus from the red box to the right.

Hmm. The expectation here is that the direction of the input has an equal weight in determining what object to select together with the distance between objects. To use your example image, if you are selecting the red box and you press right, the difference in angle between 'right' and the direction of the blue box is far smaller than the direction of 'right' and the yellow box.

Is this where it is determined whether to select a Control or not?
https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/cae3d722a3abd6d93d84a84beccc65a78948653f/scene/gui/control.cpp#L2376

> Hmm. The expectation here is that the direction of the input has an equal weight in determining what object to select together with the distance between objects. To use your example image, if you are selecting the red box and you press right, the difference in angle between 'right' and the direction of the blue box is far smaller than the direction of 'right' and the yellow box.

That makes sense, but which points should be used to indicate the direction?

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/eb5d63c7-71f2-4d32-b74b-6a47195a6a10)


I suggest to align them. For randomly placed controls, the directional offset is not easy to measure because they cannot be abstracted to a point.

> Is this where it is determined whether to select a Control or not?

Yes.

Right; thank you for asking all the good and hard questions.

I would argue that for a general system, the difference in angle of direction between the centers of the points should weigh in. As a general rule, this is most in line with the gestalt of shapes. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9100a577-7f62-4279-bc6f-22c5a8fc648b)

In the example above, I would expect the blue or yellow box to be selected before the green box. Whether it should be the blue or yellow depends on the general design decision of when to choose for a smaller distance to the control over a control that is closer to the intended direction. I can make a suggestion on that, if you'd like? I'll think about that more.

With direction between centers taken into account, even just slightly, the original issue would make the left top button absurdly out of line from the down direction:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a9675d1b-afa1-4b1e-b81a-931e948afdfa)

> In the example above, I would expect the blue or yellow box to be selected before the green box. 

If we make sure the center and width of the green box remain the same, and increase its height, what would we choose?

It is better to allow users to write custom logic. Or manually specify `focus_neighbor_*`

Hmm. The original issue I posted is so obviously wrong to me that I don't understand why you would suggest that I would write my own navigation logic or manual specify the neighbors. I'm not sure what you are suggesting. Are you suggesting that my original issue is expected and wanted behavior from the engine's perspective? That pressing down in the example below **_should_** go left?

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a9675d1b-afa1-4b1e-b81a-931e948afdfa)

Because no matter what principle you use to write it, you can always find counterexamples. I can't find the logic to cover all use cases. So I chose the simplest logic. Although it is counter-intuitive in some cases.

The reason it wasn't happening before is that it wouldn't take into account the control on the left since it was considered negative in the focus move direction.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/58caf777-02fd-4228-a101-dda2d4b30e13)

If we follow the previous logic, the controls in the `ScrollContainer` will be skipped in the above cases.

Right – you did fix some other cases which I am grateful for 🙏🏼 I am certainly not saying we should add complex logic, or that those issues you fixed are less valid than the issue I'm reporting. I just don't know what to tell you to convince you that my original issue report is unexpected and unintended behavior _for anyone_. Again, I hear you; people can make the wildest and deranged interfaces and because of that you will always be able to find counterexamples to any automatic navigation logic. But if object B is literally and precisely in the down direction from object A, and giving down input when on object A doesn't take you to object B, then that is a straight up bug and not a counter-intuitive case. If pressing down makes it go left, that isn't counter intuitive, that is wrong.

So to go back to discussing possible solutions: do you see any way at all to better integrate (even just slightly) the direction of finding a neighbor of controls?

> So to go back to discussing possible solutions: do you see any way at all to better integrate (even just slightly) the direction of finding a neighbor of controls?

I really want to, but how to allocate weights?  How much weight should be given to angles? How much weight should be given to distances? Should we use the center point to measure the offset? Should I use an offset angle or an offset distance?

The more complex the logic, the more calculations required and the slower it runs. The point is that it may not always work as expected.

If you'd like to improve it, I'd love it.

Would a possible solution be having one or two options in the project settings for how the weights should work? So depending on the preference of the developer they could decide whether the direction should be weighted higher or not?

Those are general design decisions that I firmly believe engine contributors **should** take a stance in! It's 'automatic navigation', after all, which _inherently_ means that some decisions have to be made about what automatic means.

> Should we use the center point to measure the offset?

Yes. Like I said, that is most in line with the gestalt 'rules' of shapes.

> Should I use an offset angle or an offset distance?

I don't know.

> How to allocate weights? How much weight should be given to angles? How much weight should be given to distances?

This is indeed at the heart of the issue huh? I don't think anyone can know this for sure without trying it, but here's at least two rules that I though should absolutely case where I AM certain that direction should weigh in above 
 
- Controls to which the direction of its center is > 89 degrees relative to the input direction should NOT be selected.
- Controls to which the direction of its center is the same as the input direction AND the distance is smaller than alternatives SHOULD be selected.

These two rules should in theory solve my issue, and I don't think those would require weighted decisions, right?

> Controls to which the direction of its center is > 89 degrees relative to the input direction should NOT be selected.

Still using the ScrollContainer example, if the internal control is large enough.

If we consider the overlapping situations, the situation is quite complicated and the center of the control is not appropriate for reference.

If the control in the scroll container becomes large enough, there has to be a point where automatic focus direction _should_ glance over it. 89 degrees is an absurdly high threshold, haha.

In case of overlapping controls, I am of the opinion that automatic navigation should not be able to cover all use cases. It's simply less relevant to most game UI's, as interactable elements shouldn't overlap for users to click / tap on them anyway.

> These two rules should in theory solve my issue, and I don't think those would require weighted decisions, right?

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9d870034-93a6-4dd9-9e3c-c21df449e69a)

Automatic is not a panacea. Or just drag the blue box‘s left side.

Right, these cases are still not covered unless weighted decisions about direction and distance are introduced – but the specific cases I am experiencing in the commercial game's project I just upgraded from 4.3 to 4.4 would be covered by those two rules. 😏 and to be complete, about that last example, in an ideal world I would expect 'down' would take me to the blue square and 'right' would take me to the right square. you can give me a slew of examples like these and I can tell you precisely what would make sense to me, and where 'no automatic logic' would be logical and when all the automatic logic should honestly stop working. But it's pretty hard for me to know what the underlying rules should be because I don't fully understand the technical implementation.

What I do understand is that introducing weighted decisions is scary to add to a general purpose game engine. So I too am reluctant to convince you to add them. I don't think I'm able to tell you 'distance is twice as important' without making a whole lot of try-outs with that kind of system and tweaking the numbers as I go. In making games, I have a similar approach: I make it and then tweak it until it's good.

So use `focus_neighbor_*` to manually specify where the automatic navigation cannot cover. You can use scripts to automate the process according to certain rules.

Or make the separation between individual controls equal. So it goes to the second step, comparing offsets.

For context, here is how the MRP behaves in 4.3, 4.4dev2, and 4.4stable.

Strictly speaking, I'm not sure the MRP demonstrates a regression, since in all three, the behavior is not the intuitive selection of the lower-right control. In all these videos, I am pressing the down arrow to input "ui_down".

There are at least two relevant PRs here, https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/95500 and https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/63059. (Despite the numbering, 95500 was merged first.)

**4.3** selects the **lower-left** control:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/21b6a7b7-2c28-46e6-81ef-49b266ca4193

**4.4 dev2**, which includes https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/95500, selects the **lower-left** control:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/7103ed2c-b1eb-456c-82a2-ea7a064e8407

**4.4 stable**, which includes https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/63059, selects the **upper-left** control:

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8cde99cd-3ab9-4132-9ae3-523178e09eb1

Let me briefly introduce the logic and differences in #63059:

First of all, you need to understand a few things:

1. Note that the `Rect2` applies `rotation`, `scale` and `skew`. 
2. The **global** rect is `local` to the space where the root `CanvasItem` is located.
3. Automatic focus navigation currently **only** works within the same control tree and not across trees. 
4. It is not possible to apply a **local** skew to a specific control, but you can apply a **global** skew via a `Node2D`.

The first step is to filter the controls in the direction of focus movement. This will be determined by the **global** rect of the control. (Previously, vertices were used to construct line segments for calculation. As shown in the figure below, the dotted box is the rect of the rotated control.)

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/a58634c7-671c-44d8-9648-edf74cd73a79)

The target control after the focus moves should be outside the corresponding border.  How to determine whether the control to be filtered is on the outside. It's the second difference. 

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/cf9fddea-3082-4e35-8e15-fca62a7c2d40)

According to the direction of focus movement, the control to be filtered will have two borders on the same axis. The first border is close to the negative direction of the focus movement direction, and the second border is close to the positive direction.

Previously, the comparison was the position of the first border (not considering overlap), and now it is the position of the second border (considering overlap, for `ScrollContainer` and some edge cases like rotation or skew).  This is the main reason for the different behavior in MRP. Previously, although the calculation was done using transformed points, the effect was the same as using rect.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/0fbb8032-cad5-4c7b-a64c-6048a1e68553)

In the above picture, the rects of the adjacent controls are overlapping.

If the control meets the above requirements, the closest distance will be calculated. Now it is the closest distance between rects, previously it was the closest distance between border segments (This is probably more accurate, but is of limited use since it does not take overlap into account).   

Repeat the above steps to select the nearest one from all controls. The situation in MRP ends here.

When there are multiple controls to be filtered with the **same** distance, the offset judgment will be started. Now it is based on the offset distance, previously it was based on the offset angle.

![001](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/8550f04b-9450-4b99-a90f-beabd052426a)

The figure above gives the reason for this choice. 

It's not optimal right now either, for example when moving from a corner it always moves towards the center control. This is counter-intuitive, but it ensures that you can navigate to all controls using only the arrow keys.

I believe that OP's usecase should be supported in priority compared to the last image posted by Rindbee, since a menu like that one is way more common that a cross with multiple buttons. I'd expect the cross usecase to require manual specifying of neighbours and not the other way around.

to improve on the implementation, I think first and foremost a few decisions need to be made on what scenarios and edge-cases (pun intended) automatic navigation does and doesn’t cover. some of the examples @Rindbee posted display extremely uncommon UI edge cases that in my opinion distract from much more common use-cases where people use container systems for Controls that already and automatically rule out things like overlap.

I will gladly take the lead on making a first version, and then we (and others) can both add cases to it as more comes up, and discuss each example.

and then second, I believe it to be necessary to introduce a step to the automatic navigation algorithm where it looks at the direction of a control, where direction is center to center of the global rect of a button. this seems clean concept to me right now, but maybe the MRP will change that :)

I also asked _**the**_ person who made automatic navigation in Unity how they did it, as it always worked really well for me there in the 8+ years I used Unity UI. I actually already got their elaborate response, but I'm waiting for their permission to share it here.

Here's ex-Unity's [Rune Skovbo Johansen](https://bsky.app/profile/runevision.bsky.social) on how they implemented automatic navigation between buttons in Unity UI:

> So, the user wants to change the selection in a given direction. If using a gamepad thumbstick, this could be any normalized 2D direction. Let's call this vector d.
> 
> For the current selected UI element, find a point on its edge that's in the desired input direction compared to its center. That's the starting point.
> 
> For each other interactable UI element we calculate a score and then select the one with the highest score:
> 
> We find the vector to the other UI element which is the center of the other UI element relative to the starting point. Let's call this vector o.
> 
> We want the score to be higher for elements in the right direction, and for elements that are closer. The direction can be scored as the dot product of the normalized vectors, and the distance can be scored as the inverse distance. We want to multiply these two score elements, not add them together - otherwise the relative scores of different UI elements would change depending on which units we use for distances.
> 
> Based on this, we can calculate the score as dot(d, normalize(o)) / length(o) which is equivalent to dot(d, o) / sqrLength(o)
> 
> You may want to completely disregard UI elements where the dot product is negative.
> 
> An intuition for which element this logic will choose is to imagine a circular balloon located at the starting point. As the balloon grows in size in the direction of d, the first UI element whose center is touched by the balloon circle is the one that's selected.
> 
> I hope that helps!

> For the current selected UI element, find a point on its edge that's in the desired input direction compared to its center. That's the starting point.

This is indeed a good technique, and the equal-score line will be more inclined to the direction.
[Above](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/issues/103895#issuecomment-2972567846) is the new algorithm that came to mind. @AdriaandeJongh Thoughts?

Since I have a GitHub account too, I might as well jump into this discussion, given the algorithm I came up with and implemented for Unity is discussed.

> The equal score line will be a circle.

Yeah, I described that in the explanation of mine that was quoted:

> An intuition for which element this logic will choose is to imagine a circular balloon located at the starting point. As the balloon grows in size in the direction of d, the first UI element whose center is touched by the balloon circle is the one that's selected.

That's another way to talk about the same thing as the equal score line.

> This algorithm is suitable for actions that can be aimed (using axes), that is, it focuses on ensuring the correct direction, You need to aim for the center of the target control to navigate.

You do not need to aim for the correct (precise) direction for it to work well. Unity uses it for four-directional inputs, and it works very well for that use case too. It's just general enough to work well for thumbstick or other any-direction inputs too, and make use of the extra precision there.

> In this case, maybe using bubble blowing algorithm might be a better approach.

Ok, let's refer to the two algorithms as balloon vs bubble.

They converge towards the same thing at large distances; the primary difference is how they behave close to the starting control.

I can't off the top of my head think of use cases where one works clearly better than the other, so it would be nice to see various configurations of buttons and see how the two approaches might differ in behavior.

What I can say is that the bubble approach is highly tied to rectangular shapes and four-directional input, so if you want to support thumbstick input too, that would require a completely separate approach, which could give rise to unintuitive differences in behavior that might be perceived as bugs. The balloon approach on the other hand works well for four directions and analog directions alike. Here's some other things to consider:

- Might you ever want to support other control shapes than rectangles? Can be done graphics-wise already of course, but this might be undermined by the navigation logic if it strongly assumes every control is a rectangle.
- How should rectangular controls that are not screen-aligned work for four-directional input? For example if they're rotated by 45 degrees. This is trivial to handle with the balloon approach as it's not tied to the orientation of a rectangle.

Just some food for thought and things to consider.

We may prefer visual correctness, at least to ensure that there are no counterintuitive situations. There are three main things here: the starting point (can it represent the source control?), the end point (can it represent the target control?), and the direction offset weight. When aiming with a gamepad, the above is less important than the user aiming. Because the user's attention may be focused on aiming. The circular equal score line can balance the deviations in all directions. This makes intuitive sense. But if only four-directional inputs are allowed, all of the above may be more important. Because there is no more detailed guidance on the aiming direction. You can find counterintuitive examples beyond the equal score lines when using balloons. Especially if the height of the source control in the graph is high enough, the controls on both sides may score higher on the right side than on the slightly left side. As shown in the figure below. $Q$ is on the circle, $M$ is inside the circle, and its score should be higher than $Q$. This would be counterintuitive if it happened in an area where the edge was moving in that direction. If it occurs in the more distal areas on both sides, it may be more acceptable. This is the change in the bubble. In the case of four-directional inputs, it may be more like starting from an edge rather than a point.

> We may prefer visual correctness, at least to ensure that there are no counterintuitive situations.

When it comes to heuristics for intuition, I think the term "correctness" isn't very helpful, as it's hard, if not impossible, to determine objectively what is more intuitive. So let's keep this grounded: Different approaches have different pros and cons with respect to which situations they can handle in a way that people will arguably find intuitive.

Ultimately, the only way to verify the intuitiveness though is involve large amounts of users. This can be via user tests of various kinds, but how the questions/tests are phrased and structured can have large effects on the results. Or one can rely on user feedback over time for already released features, but here there's biases too, such as users being more prone to submit feedback if they have issues than if things are working fine for them.

When it comes to just us discussing things here, the best we can hope for is that we reach some consensus, and that if we do reach consensus on what we here find more intuitive in more situations, hopefully most users would agree. But none of that has anything to do with correctness.

> When aiming with a gamepad, the above is less important than the user aiming. Because the user's attention may be focused on aiming.

I don't follow that logic. When different controls have different shapes and sizes, it's no more given to a user what "direction" one control is compared to another than it is with four-directional input.

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6de464a3-dec1-4734-869d-d278c60ce785)

In the image above, how do we know if one arrow or the other represents the user's intuition for switching focus from the bottom control to the middle-left one?

For this reason, we can't rely much more on user aiming with freeform directions than we can with four-directional input. In either case, we need to determine what "aiming upwards" means with regard to which control gets selected, and I don't see why a user's intuition for that would change depending on what input method they use.

> You can find counterintuitive examples beyond the equal score lines when using balloons.

Possibly! But I think to talk about what examples are intuitive or not, we should use examples with control rectangles drawn, not just points. Since the control shapes can highly affect people's intuition for these things.

>  Q is on the circle, M is inside the circle, and its score should be higher than Q .

This is true, but I think your illustration is misleading. If M and Q were both slightly inside the circle by the same distance, Q would be hit by the balloon first, since it grows from the left side, not from the center.

It's best to draw the circle such that no points are inside, since it's the shape of it when it hits the first point that matters, not its shape when it has grown further beyond that. In the image below, the black circle is the "balloon" grown to the size where it first touches a point (point M, though it's close enough that it's hard to see).

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/32e60d89-78e4-433c-9865-27f7ff5f4c9b)

It's possible the balloon approach could be improved by considering collissions with the edge of other controls rather than the center of controls. At Unity we never implemented such a change, since to my knowledge we didn't get complaints about the behavior as it was. But it might well work better.

So I would suggest:

- Consider the balloon approach also where it's the first touched control edge that's selected, rather than the first touched control center.
- Construct examples with control configurations (rectangles) that show how the different algorithms would fare in different situations - not artificial math diagrams that only consider points, since it's about intuition, not pure math.
- Address my question about rectangular controls that are not screen-aligned, and include such examples in the comparison of how the different approaches fare.

Let me also say that I do think the bubble approach has some very desirable traits.

If we did not need to consider gamepad input, and if we did not need to consider controls that are not screen-aligned rectangles, then I agree it would most likely be better than the balloon approach. But since IMO we *do* need an approach that works for any-directional input too, and we *should* consider rectangles that are not aligned with the screen, the current bubble-approach's high coupling with a control's rectangle shape and orientation gives it some large drawbacks.

Ideally we'd find some way to generalize the bubble approach, or something like it, to work for any direction rather than being tied to a rectangle's four sides. The balloon approach and bubble approach are already somewhat similar. It's possible there's other "expanding circle" approaches that retain the advantages of both approaches at once.

> > Q is on the circle, M is inside the circle, and its score should be higher than Q . > > This is true, but I think your illustration is misleading. If M and Q were both slightly inside the circle by the same distance, Q would be hit by the balloon first, since it grows from the left side, not from the center. > > It's best to draw the circle such that no points are inside, since it's the shape of it when it hits the first point that matters, not its shape when it has grown further beyond that. In the image below, the black circle is the "balloon" grown to the size where it first touches a point (point M, though it's close enough that it's hard to see). > That is a random picture, the following is a carefully designed one. $Q$ is the tangent point, which is the first point touched when it touches the red line, and $P$ is the midpoint. The bubble doesn't solve this problem, it just puts them far away on the sides. The higher the score of a point, the smaller the radius of the circle of its equal score line, and the point is contacted first. **The advantage of a circle is that it expands twice as fast in the direction as it expands along the sides.** > If we did not need to consider gamepad input, and if we did not need to consider controls that are not screen-aligned rectangles, then I agree it would most likely be better than the balloon approach. But since IMO we do need an approach that works for any-directional input too, and we should consider rectangles that are not aligned with the screen, the current bubble-approach's high coupling with a control's rectangle shape and orientation gives it some large drawbacks. In fact, the coordinate system can be converted, and after the conversion, the input in any direction is similar to the input in 4 directions: Rect can be constructed along the navigation direction $\vec{d}$ and its normal vector. Overlapping can be allowed and some preprocessing can be done on the overlap.

Ok, so the proposed solution to address mismatch of a control's rect and the direction of the four control directions is to use enclosing bounding boxes. Note though that this can cause controls to inflate a lot in size, and for rotated long thin controls, it can result in neighboring controls being fully inside the current control's bounding box. Just one more thing to keep in mind for pros and cons of various approaches.

So I guess what's left is to get a better idea of what might feel more intuitive is to look at a large variety of example control layouts and determine how the various approaches would behave in each. There's plenty of inspiration of irregular control layouts here: https://www.gameuidatabase.com/index.php?scrn=64

I really appreciate the discussion here. The math is a bit above my level of intelligence, but I hope I'm still able to contribute to the discussion meaningfully.

> The advantage of a circle is that it expands twice as fast in the direction as it expands along the sides.

This sounds great and on the right path.

re: enclosing bounding boxes: I do understand why there is the tendency to optimize for axis aligned bounding boxes because A) keyboard input uses 4 directions and B) rectangles have 4 sides and all Controls are rectangles (right?)

However, if I [look at this image](https://www.gameuidatabase.com/index.php?scrn=64&autoload=41995) of a skill tree, it's easy to argue that **_IF_** the player is playing with a controller using a joystick that can point at any direction, it would with no doubt be better to allow for more directionality in the solution. Here's two ideas for methods on how that could work:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6af4dba4-ed24-40b5-90fc-4b45cf80efad)

Method A explained: point A is the center of Control rect, the line AB is the direction of input, point B where the direction of input hits the rectangle edge, and where circle C is the visualization of the circle that grows in the direction of AB and scores the touching controls.

Method B explained: same as method A, but where point B is a point on circle / ellipse Z which in turn is a circle / ellipse that crosses all centers of the edges of the Control's rect. this supposedly would allow a bit more leniency and flexibility, because not all UI's are rectangle focussed.

And note that both these methods would also work when the rect of the Control is rotated:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/f5c3e9d3-c72b-4de4-8bde-e2aa4bf3e66b)

I don't know how different this is from the solutions proposed by @Rindbee and @runevision? Perhaps it's not far off, in which case I would argue to allow for multiple directions! If it is completely different and requires a very different implementation, then I'd argue to stick to axis aligned bounding boxes and optimize for that – losing the ability to automatically navigate to Controls in any direction.

> I don't know how different this is from the solutions proposed by [@Rindbee](https://github.com/Rindbee) and [@runevision](https://github.com/runevision)?

Unity does something like your method A - finds a point on the rectangle edge. There's some scaling involved so that if the input direction is at 45 degrees relative to the rect, it'll find the corner (regardless of the scaling of the rect). But I'm not sure if the finer details here are super important. Just make a note of the point that the direction from the rect center to the starting point, and the further direction from there, don't necessarily have to be exactly the same.

> Perhaps it's not far off, in which case I would argue to allow for multiple directions! If it is completely different and requires a very different implementation, then I'd argue to stick to axis aligned bounding boxes and optimize for that – losing the ability to automatically navigate to Controls in any direction.

So Unity only has one method (the "balloon" method I described in the quite you posted) which is used for both any-directional input like thumbstick and four-directional input like keyboard arrows.

My impression is that @Rindbee is not happy with the properties of this method for four-directional input, hence the discussion of alternatives. But those alternatives are highly tailored to four-directional input *only*.

If it was me, I would focus on any-directional input first, since it has to be done *anyway*. If the balloon method is used for any-directional input, we know that it works well enough for four-directional input too to be used for it in Unity and hence in lots of shipped game titles. With that out of the way, here is the code I implemented for the balloon algorithm in general:
```gdscript
func _input(input_dir: Vector2, nodes: Array[Control], current_node: Control) -> Control:
	# 1. Compute the starting point.
	var control_rect := current_node.get_global_rect()
	var starting_point := intersect_rect_with_dir(control_rect, control_rect.get_center(), input_dir)
	
	# 2. Calculate score iteratively, storing a pair of <controlNode, score> for the lowest score
	var candidate = Candidate.new(current_node, starting_point)
	for node in nodes:
		var node_rect := Rect2(Vector2.ZERO, node.size)
		var node_point = calculate_candidate_point(starting_point, input_dir, node_rect, node.get_global_transform())
		var node_distance =  node_point - starting_point
		var other_candidate = Candidate.new(
			node,
			node_point,
			input_dir.dot(node_distance) / node_distance.length_squared()
		)
		if candidate.is_higher(other_candidate):
			candidate = other_candidate
	
	# 3. Return the candidate node only if the score is positive;
	#    otherwise, maintain focus on current node
	return candidate.node if candidate.score > 0 else current_node
```

The three different variations only differ on how they calculate candidate positions:

- **Center point**: Returns the control's rect center point ([source](https://github.com/rsubtil/godot-control-focus-tests/blob/main/implementations/BalloonCenter.gd))
- **Edge point towards center**: Calculates the intersection between the starting point and the node's rect when pointing it to the center ([source](https://github.com/rsubtil/godot-control-focus-tests/blob/main/implementations/BalloonEdgeTowardsCenter.gd))
- **Edge point**: Calculates true edge point intersection ([source](https://github.com/rsubtil/godot-control-focus-tests/blob/main/implementations/BalloonEdge.gd), based on @runevision [gist](https://gist.github.com/runevision/970445fa11280def3e8be241fd3dc720))

With regard to calculating the start position for rotated rectangles, (and arbitrary input directions), here's an illustration for how I recommend doing that (which is also how it's done in Unity's uGUI UI system). Right. Thinking about it, I think there's a trivial fix. Exclude all controls whose center is _behind_ the starting point. By behind, I mean that the dot product of the input direction, and the direction from the starting point to the control center is negative.

This check happens implicitly for the "balloon with center points" approach, but not for the others. Why involve the control center point for the approaches where the score evaluation is not based on the center? Well, I think the center is still relevant to a certain intuition, even if it's not the bases for the calculated score. And I think the focus going to a control whose center is behind the starting point will generally feel wrong, since it'll overall feel like the focus moved in a very different direction than what was inputted.

Since the check is computationally trivial, I'd recommend doing it as the first thing, before calculating the score (which is of course not necessary if the "behind" check fails).

I've found this very interesting thread recently after battling with arrow key focus navigation quite a bit in Godot. For blind gamers, keyboard arrow navigation is the primary way to navigate through menus besides controller input, and the way it currently works makes it hard to create an intuitively usable menu. I may be wrong, but while I appreciate that unity's algorithm makes focus navigation more intuitive, it will still create accessibility issues if the accessibility tree order is ignored with a custom algorithm. Take the following common situation: some buttons in a vertical menu, and a few buttons in a horizontal position: Arrow-keying down will end you up at the confirm button, and skips the cancel button. Tabbing down will get you to the cancel button, then the confirm button. Tab follows the accessibility tree, arrow keys do not. This causes blind arrow-key users to completely miss certain buttons if you're not careful and meticulous with your UI setup. While you can correct the navigation flow with focus neighbors, this is very volatile and easy to introduce bugs when that UI is modified, especially through code. It will eventually result in more games being less accessible, and create more work for developers to make their games blind accessible. Given the current predicament, I've tried to tell players to use tab in my game for navigation and arrows for widgets that inherently use 2d navigation like grids and tab views, but in the end most users (blind or not) generally do not use tab to navigate in games. They use arrow keys. Would it not make more sense to just follow the accessibility tree for arrow keys as well by default? And if you do need some sort of more complicated 2-dimensional navigation, set focus neighbors and apply the balloon algorithm. Then there are the special cases: grid container, scroll container, tab container, foldable container. These each behave differently in the web and I think we would do well to more closely adopt the web standards on this. Though there is one major difference there: people DO use tab to get around the web, and scroll containers deserve their own discussion on whether they should only scroll (if they just contain text) or move the focus on their children (if they just contain buttons). But generally I think looking at the web and how focus moves there is the more accessible way.

Apologies for the delay in summing up this as a new proposal, but it is now finally completed 😌 . I've cc'ed some main participants from here, but everyone feel free to give your feedback on the proposal.

I ended up ditching the "center" point variation of the algorithm, as it fails pretty bad on Adriaan's 4th scenario, where the current algorithm succeeds, so it would likely perform worse in some scenarios, for little performance improvement it might have compared to the edge algorithm.

@Josvanegmond while I haven't had much experience developing UI functionality for visually-impaired users, I did work on a past project where I had a fully blind user. At the time what seemed to me the most fundamental rule is that, for accessibility purposes, UI navigation needs to be 1 dimensional, as opposed to the usual 2D approach.

Seeing how this algorithm heavily relies on 2D visualization, I don't think defaulting to the accessibility tree would result in intuitive scenarios, as both approaches will naturally be quite different. The accessibility tree maps the 2D environment in a 1D environment, attempting to make deterministic movement for next/previous elements. This is more intuitive for visually-impaired users, but not so much for 2D navigation, which this algorithm relies even more than the current one. Regardless, I agree this accessibility topic should be reviewed if the proposal is accepted, although that's best left for someone with more experience than me.

In my project I decided to remap Up/Down arrows from `ui_up`/`ui_down` to `ui_focus_prev`/`ui_focus_next`, and I had very positive feedback from that design choice. Might be something to consider in your case?

@rsubtil thanks for elaborating on that. I have come to the same conclusions while testing with many blind gamers. Treating the UI as 1-dimensional is quite important. Wether buttons are vertically or horizontally laid out does not really matter. Both left and down arrows should advance the focus through he list of buttons. 

Grids and other natively 2-dimensional navigation components need a different strategy, thats where the balloon solution makes perfect sense.

 I advocate to make 1-dimensional navigation the standard behavior so developers dont have to do anything special to make their navigation more accessible. It already is by default. And this kind of choices in the engine is very important to increase accessibility in general.
